title: Akiva's last Shema (Berakhot 61b)
hookLine: executed by Rome, Akiva dies saying the Shema, finally loving God "with all thy soul"

cards: Rome has forbidden the teaching of Torah. Rabbi Akiva gathers students anyway, in public. A man named Pappos ben Yehudah asks whether he isn't afraid.
Akiva answers with a parable. A fox by a river sees fish darting from place to place. Why are you running?
From the nets, they say. Come up on the dry land, says the fox, and live with me. And the fish answer: if we're afraid in the water where we live, how much more on land, where we die.
Torah, Akiva says, is our water. Not long after, he is arrested.

teach.b: The Talmud tells what came next, in tractate Berakhot, page sixty-one. Akiva is taken out to be put to death, and the Roman executioners tear at his flesh with iron combs.
It's the hour for the Shema, the verses from Deuteronomy said morning and evening: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." And Akiva says it.
His students can't bear it: our teacher, even this far? Akiva answers, in paraphrase: all my life one phrase troubled me.

The next verse says, "thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." With all thy soul, the rabbis taught, means even if God takes your soul, your life.

All my days I wondered when I would have the chance to keep this. Now that it has come, shall I not keep it? He draws out the last word of the first line, echad, one, and his life leaves him as he says it.
The Talmud adds that a voice from heaven spoke: happy are you, Rabbi Akiva. The Talmud doesn't make it easy: in the same passage the angels protest: is this Torah, and is this its reward?
But at its heart is a man who studied one phrase for years and, in the worst moment of his life, found that it fit.
Akiva's last Shema is the ordinary Shema, said morning and evening in Jewish prayer, said all the way through.

how: Jews say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime, with a custom of covering the eyes for the first line and lengthening the word echad, and it is traditionally said at the end of life.

o: listen, the first word of the Shema's first line
love, the word that opens the very next verse
one, the last word of the Shema's first line

games.q: Akiva's last Shema — tap the pairs.
p: afraid in the water, more so on land
even if God takes your life

s: Akiva stopped teaching when Rome forbade it
he kept teaching in public and answered with the parable of the fox and the fish.
Akiva died saying the word echad, one
the Talmud says his life left him as he drew out the last word of the Shema's first line.
the Talmud tells the story as simple triumph
in the same passage the angels protest: is this Torah, and is this its reward?

games.q: the fox invites the fish to leave the dangerous river and live on dry land. you're the fish. what do you say?
o: accept, and climb out to safety.
if we're afraid in the water, how much more on land.
ask the fox to remove the nets.
games.why: the fish stay in the water. in Akiva's parable, Torah is the water: dangerous to stay in, deadly to leave.

practice: Sit tall; some people cover their eyes with one hand for the first line of the Shema, to shut out everything else.

If you pray, say it slowly, Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one, and let the last word stretch the way Akiva stretched it. If you don't, hold the line as Akiva's words, and let your breath go long on that one word.

wordCard.voice: Echad. The Hebrew word for one, the last word of the Shema, which Rabbi Akiva drew out as he died under Roman torture.

orig.note: Hebrew: with all your soul, the phrase from the Shema that Akiva said he waited his whole life to keep.

carryVoice: Your line: with all your soul. Torah, Akiva said, was his water. Day nine hundred four, in the books.
